title: Logistic Regression: The Sigmoid 🧬
description: Understand odds, log‑odds, and the sigmoid function that turns a line into a probability.

slides.title: From Line to Probability ⚖️
slides.content:
# Logistic Regression = Linear Model + Sigmoid

Despite its name, logistic regression is a **classification** algorithm. It predicts the probability that an instance belongs to the positive class (e.g., “yes”).

First, it computes a linear combination of features:
```
z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₚxₚ + b
```
Then it squeezes z through the **sigmoid** (logistic) function to get a value between 0 and 1:
```
σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)
```
Interpretation: σ(z) is the estimated probability P(y=1 | x).

slides.title: The Sigmoid Shape 📈
slides.content:
# S‑Curve Magic

- When z is very large (e.g., +∞), e⁻ᶻ ≈ 0 → σ(z) ≈ 1.
- When z is very small (e.g., −∞), e⁻ᶻ → ∞ → σ(z) ≈ 0.
- When z = 0, σ(0) = 0.5.

The sigmoid smoothly maps any real number to a probability. This is the heart of logistic regression.

It also has a beautiful derivative: σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), which makes gradient descent easy.

quizData.question: What is the output of σ(0)?

slides.title: Odds and Log‑Odds 🎲
slides.content:
# Another Perspective

Logistic regression models the **log‑odds** of the positive class as a linear function:

```
odds = P(y=1) / (1 − P(y=1))
log‑odds = ln(odds) = w·x + b
```

So we can write:
```
P(y=1) = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) = eᶻ / (1 + eᶻ)
```

This means a one‑unit increase in feature xⱼ multiplies the odds by e^(wⱼ). This is why logistic regression is popular in fields like medicine — odds ratios are easy to interpret.

slides.title: Sigmoid in Python 🐍
Remember 📌
slides.content:
## Threshold = 0.5
Usually we predict class 1 if P(y=1) ≥ 0.5, which is equivalent to z ≥ 0 (since σ(0)=0.5). The line z=0 is the **decision boundary**.
